cards.source_text: A worsening convergence of drought driven by climate change, epidemic disease, and state neglect is creating a severe health emergency for the Indigenous Matsés people in the Peruvian Amazon. Mongabay staff writer Aimee Gabay traveled to Matsés territory to investigate the environmental threats to the region. Instead, she found Matsés communities suffering from severe outbreaks of malaria and hepatitis B, she tells host Mike DiGirolamo in a recent episode of the Mongabay Newscast. “When I arrived, interview after interview, I was asking questions about environmental threats, and people were like, ‘Well, people are dying on the streets’,” Gabay says. “And it got to the point where I was like I’m asking the wrong questions here.” According to Gabay, the Matsés officially initiated contact with evangelical missionaries in 1969 to escape escalating violence from rubber tappers, loggers and military bombardments. However, the contact exposed them to infectious diseases. Roberto Necca Tumio Unan, a Matsés elder born before contact was initiated, told Gabay that entire families began dying shortly after contact from diseases previously unknown to them. “They don’t have the immunological defenses to be able to fight these diseases that maybe, for us, we are constantly exposed to,” Gabay says. Now, the health crisis is compounded by droughts in the Amazon. Low river levels restrict boat navigation, the primary transit route in the roadless region, preventing healthcare workers from entering remote villages and blocking sick villagers from reaching medical care. Matsés chief Leo Chuma Teca Beso told Gabay that he traveled to Iquitos in northeastern Peru and capital Lima to plead for state intervention, reporting that sick community members are dying on streets due to advanced hepatitis B complications such as cirrhosis. While Peru’s Ministry of Health (MINSA) previously reported zero hepatitis B deaths among the Matsés, chief Leo said this figure reflects a lack of testing. Civil society health brigades have only screened around 20% of the population so far, identifying 17 hepatitis B cases, according to the health ministry. Gabay says that MINSA officials cited budget constraints and geographic remoteness as reasons for the delays in healthcare aid and support. cards.source_text: She is an unlikely harbinger of the climate emergency: a venomous black and yellow spider who spins mysterious patterns in her webs and eats her mates for breakfast. Native to mainland Europe, north Africa and Asia, the Argiope bruennichi – commonly known as a wasp spider – is rarely seen in the north and west of Britain. But a fully grown female has been spotted in Cheshire for the first time by conservationists from Chester zoo, who stumbled across the large, brightly striped arachnid in a rewilded field. The species, which mimics a wasp to deter predators, is thought to be the latest “climate refugee” extending its range northwards as the planet heats. Females can grow to about 2cm in body length, making it one of the largest spiders found in the UK. “You know your big, chunky house spiders – the ones you think are massive and frighten the life out of you in your living room? A female wasp spider is probably a bit bigger than those,” said Scott Wilson, head of field programmes at the zoo. Although they are not dangerous to humans, they often attack and cannibalise their mates during or after copulation. Males usually reach only about a quarter of the length of the females and studies have found that up to 80% die after their first mating attempt while the rest die after their second. Their body then provides the female with valuable protein as she produces her eggs. It is not yet known how the spread of the wasp spider, which was also revealed to be moving west into counties such as Worcestershire, Herefordshire and Warwickshire last week, will affect local ecosystems in the north. “That’s quite often the risk with these ecological shifts – we don’t know what the implications will be,” said Wilson. The spider recorded in Cheshire was discovered on the Chester zoo estate during a routine “bioblitz” to monitor biodiversity on 80 hectares of land being set aside for nature. An expert from the British Arachnological Society later confirmed it was the first recorded sighting of the species in the county. “It was quite easy to spot,” said Wilson. “It’s a really big, colourful spider and the webs are huge and distinctive … They have this thick zigzag, which some people think is there to reflect UV light and attract insects, but nobody really knows.” The wider zoo estate, which includes wet meadows,grasslands, woodlands and orchards, already supports a diverse range of important UK species, such as great crested newts, badgers and harvest mice. cards.source_text: A magical film that explores the wonders of the deep sea through the eyes of a team of scientists and an underwater robot called Isis will be shown in selected cinemas across the UK next month. The documentary, How Deep Is Your Love, offers a playful, irreverent and bittersweet look at our anthropocentric view of Earth, as it switches perspective from humans to deep sea animals and back again. It follows a research team from the Natural History Museum (NHM) in London, who sail for 12 days to reach a remote region called the Clarion Clipperton Zone, a biodiversity-rich area of the Pacific between Hawaii and Mexico. It takes Isis five hours to make the 3-mile (5km) descent to the bottom of this harsh world, where sunlight cannot penetrate, and where nodules rich in minerals mark it out as a hotspot for industrial mining. It is a race against time for the scientists to identify new species before deep sea mining threatens to wipe out fragile ecosystems for ever. Scientists estimate that only 0.001% of the deep sea floor – categorised by some as more than 500 metres below the sea’s surface, where sunlight fades to total darkness – has been observed by humans. The film is an ode, says director Eleanor Mortimer, to the taxonomists and biologists who spend “hours and hours counting the legs of a minuscule animal you can’t even see with the naked eye” and to the strange creatures of the abyssal plain, of which we know so little. Even when painstakingly identified, and DNA collected, it can take up to 14 years to name a species, Mortimer says. “It’s the challenge of the deep sea,” says Mortimer, who shares the scientists’ desire to demystify life in the deep. “Most people never go there, and yet it’s a huge part of our planet we need to connect with. That was the motive behind the film. I want people to fall in love with the deep sea, I want people to connect with it.” She became “obsessed” with the region, but could not work out how to make a film until, by chance, she met Muriel Rabone, the film’s science adviser and co-producer, who told Mortimer about the NHM team. “Their love and curiosity and excitement have become infectious,” says Mortimer. Most of the film takes place at sea, or at the International Seabed Authority (ISA) in Jamaica, which regulates activities in the seabed beyond national jurisdiction. cards.source_text: Former United Nations climate chief Christiana Figueres has been named the recipient of the inaugural Jane Goodall Earth Medal, which honors those who “unite science, courage and responsibility.” Goodall, a primatologist, conservationist and a persistent voice of hope, died in October 2025 at the age of 91. Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and led negotiations for the 2015 Paris climate agreement, discussed the award on the Mongabay Newscast hosted by Mike DiGirolamo. cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 28 minute listen In late summer 2023, I found myself in a smoke shop looking at a package of ‘magic mushroom’ gummies. That phrase, magic mushrooms, usually calls to mind one type of mushroom: those containing psilocybin, the compound showing promise as a therapy for depression, addiction and other psychopathologies. But these gummies were not psilocybin. Instead, the packaging described Amanita muscaria, the red-capped, white-spotted toadstool of fairy-tale forests, iPhone keyboards and Super Mario. I knew a little about the folklore of Amanita muscaria. I had first seen it discussed in an episode of the show Hamilton’s Pharmacopeia (2016-21), which begins with a claim I now hear often: that Amanita muscaria may be among the oldest human intoxicants. The New York banker-turned-ethnomycologist R Gordon Wasson, whose Life magazine essay from 1957 introduced psilocybin mushrooms to a mass Western audience, certainly took this idea seriously. In his book Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality (1968), he argued that the Vedic soma – a ritual drink in ancient Indian religions – was made from Amanita muscaria. The mushroom has also been linked, sometimes carefully and sometimes wildly, to the origins of Santa Claus, Viking berserkers and even Christianity. Some believe its other name, ‘fly agaric’, stems from its use as a natural pesticide for house flies; the word muscaria is also derived from the Latin word musca, meaning fly. Some scholars have linked Amanita muscaria to Lewis Carroll’s mushroom scene in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865), in which the Caterpillar tells Alice that ‘one side’ of the mushroom will make her taller and the other shorter, though Carroll does not identify a species. But I wasn’t standing in that smoke shop holding one of these products as a folklorist or looking to lose myself in Carroll’s ‘golden afternoon’. I am a public-health scientist, and my questions were pragmatic: what exactly was in this package? Could it hurt someone? Were these products legal? The first thing I did was what I usually do. I went to the scientific literature. And down the rabbit hole I tumbled. Although manufacturers use the term ‘magic mushrooms’, the main psychoactive compound in Amanita muscaria is not pharmacologically interchangeable with psilocybin; the two drugs do not act on the brain in the same way. The body converts psilocybin into psilocin, the substance that actually produces its psychedelic effects. Psilocin switches

cards.source_text: Critical theorists like Theodor Adorno may have overreached in claiming that all mass culture is mediocre, mechanized propaganda made to justify the status quo. But that doesn’t mean they were entirely wrong. Over and over we see even the most subversive art, literature, film, and music has a way of being tamed and Bowdlerized. Global mega-corporate industries don’t need to censor what they don’t like; they only need to buy it, rebrand it, or price it out of reach. So what? Why do we need challenging, independent art when we have endless entertainment? Is the concept a nostalgic, elitist, Eurocentric idea? Artists have justified the need for art since antiquity, with poetic and logical arguments of every kind. But Dada artists of the early 20th century broke ranks, building their movement on the insight that no defense could possibly mean anything when it came to art’s purpose, especially in the face of the technocratic slaughter of World War I. When the hyperrationalism of modernity led to mass death and destruction, the only humane response was to declare war on rationalization—to “destroy the hoaxes of reason,” as French artist Jean Arp put it. “For the disillusioned artists of the Dada movement,” the Museum of Modern Art explains, “the war merely confirmed the degradation of social structures that led to such violence: corrupt and nationalist politics, repressive social values, and unquestioning conformity of culture and thought.” Dada took a combative stance against, for one thing, the insistence that art justify its existence to win establishment approval. “All activity is vain,” declared poet Tristan Tzara in his 1918 “Dada Manifesto,” including the “monetary system, pharmaceutical product, or a bare leg advertising the ardent sterile spring…. cards.source_text: For Abidin, a Balik elder who lives in East Kalimantan in Borneo, Indonesia, the sounds of nature aren’t merely a backdrop but a vital part of how he navigates the world. But as the rainforest around him has become more developed, the calls of creatures once heard everywhere have grown scarce. And that process is speeding up. To relieve Indonesia’s capital city of Jakarta, which is sinking due to overdevelopment and vulnerable to climate change, the government is building a new one, Nusantara, close to Abidin’s home. The noise of construction and city life is beginning to overpower the soundscape he relies on, and researchers suspect they may already be pushing wildlife away. In this short documentary, the US director Leah Varjacques traces an effort to record the sounds of the rainforest before they’re altered forever. The film follows Abidin working with a research team that includes Wendy Erb, a bioacoustic scientist from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in New York, to collect audio from caves, treetops and everywhere in between. In doing so, they hope to create a record for posterity so that the rainforest’s soundscapes – and the culture and ancestral knowledge embedded within them – are never fully erased.

cards.source_text: Listen to this essay 22 minute listen How tightly should you hold your beliefs? You face the question several times a week without noticing. Hold them too loosely and you don’t stand for anything, hold them too tightly and you become the sort of person no argument can reach. Most of us swing between the two and have no vocabulary for the ground in between. A Roman lawyer worked one out, under pressure far worse than anything we are likely to face, and it is still the best answer available. The time is early 45 BCE, the place a villa near Lucrine Lake, northwest of Naples, in southern Italy. One of the most fascinating and controversial figures in the entirety of Western history, Marcus Tullius Cicero, is finishing writing a book that will be known as the Academica, where he explains the nature of sceptical philosophy and why it is so crucial not just to the advancement of human knowledge, but to living a good life. It is a strange moment to retire into one’s villa to write. The Roman Republic, so beloved by Cicero, is about to be destroyed by aspiring autocrats: Julius Caesar, a longtime friend and now a political opponent, has declared himself dictator for life, a move that will soon lead to his assassination on the Ides of March 44 BCE. On the personal front, Cicero has recently divorced Terentia, his wife of 30 years, and a few months ago his beloved daughter Tullia died from complications following childbirth. You would think a man whose private and public worlds are collapsing so dramatically would hardly have the focus to write philosophy. Yet for Cicero such writing is a form of therapy, and the treatises he produces will influence medieval Christians, Renaissance authors, and the Founders of the American Republic. Cicero managed all this because of his adopted philosophy, ‘Academic Skepticism’, so-called because it characterised, for the period from 266 to 90 BCE, the Academy originally founded by Plato. He used to be treated as a mere populariser, a gifted Roman relaying Greek ideas he did not really own, but scholars abandoned that uncharitable verdict decades ago as it became clear that Cicero argued and decided among his sources rather than simply transcribing them. He also built a Latin philosophical vocabulary from scratch, and much of the abstract terminology of European thought descends from his coinages. cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. So influential was Jugend that Art Nouveau in Germany became known as Jugendstil. The Oxford Critical and Cultural History of Modernist Magazines writes, “Among Jugend’s most important qualities—indeed, an essential aspect of Art Nouveau and its German equivalent Jugendstil—was its brilliant escapism.” Founded in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the magazine was “from the start a venue to promote the new cultural Renaissance without recourse to the established ‘vintage’ art.” (See its very first cover right above.) cards.source_text: AK Blakemore’s third novel tells the story of the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, when commoners of all classes – not only peasants, but merchants, servants, smugglers, and some local lords and officials – rebelled at the imposition of a poll tax and rampaged through southern England, burning records of debts, killing their oppressors and laying waste to their homes. The book closely follows the events of the rebellion’s 16 days, employing a vast array of points of view, including the young king Richard II, several of his courtiers, dozens of elements of the rebellious Commons, a porpoise and a runaway horse. The title suggests the novel’s portrayal of these events as an inevitable reckoning; a “doom painting” was a picture of the Last Judgment on the wall of a medieval church. As a book of this scope must be, it’s a doorstopper. As any novel by Blakemore will be, it’s dazzlingly rich in lexical glamour, and this is likely to be any reader’s lasting impression of the book. Sometimes it feels as if the author is out to use every word in the English language in a startling, aestheticised, puckish way that expands both the word and the world. The result can be joyously silly. Who else would give us slugs that “blurb their elementary forms from out of the undergrowth to begin a dank and toothless festa”, or “lunar-brilliantined mud”? But there is also gravity and passion here, especially when she intimately imagines the lives of the commoners: “they rise, to fry eggs in butter and pork fat; they rise, to whet knives on scarred stone; they rise, to braid the manes of their draught horses; they rise, to count arrows; they rise, setting aside their glitchy dreams of hairy stars and blue-skinned devils; they rise, fearful and powerful, into the bright day.” The cheekily anachronistic appearance of “glitchy” in this medieval scene is typical of Blakemore’s method. All forms of language, high and low, archaic and modern, are here. Her use of detail to convey a historical scene is also extraordinary: the barber’s chair where “a crowd has gathered beneath the ribboned pole to watch the draining of a cyst”; the brewer with “a grotty beard, chlorotic with hops, [that] hangs down almost to his belt”; or “the horseflies waltzing over the liquefying flesh of severed heads”. Blakemore is less successful in the traditional novelistic areas of plot and character. The primary figure throughout is legendary rebel leader Wat Tyler. cards.source_text: Kate Mosse’s new book is a love-song to West Sussex, part of a series designed to bring out its authors’ personal connections to a home landscape. It began last year, with Michael Morpurgo welcoming spring in Devon, where he has lived – at the farm that inspired War Horse – for over 50 years; and then Val McDermid celebrating winter in Scotland, where she grew up and still lives. Bernardine Evaristo will explore summer soon – but, meanwhile, we have Mosse, also deeply and endearingly rooted in her chosen patch. Mosse grew up in the village of Fishbourne. She now lives in Chichester, where she got to know her husband when they revised for A-levels in the shadow of the Bishop’s Palace, and held hands when she turned 17 on the day of the city’s annual Sloe Fair. Twenty-three years later, they celebrated her 40th there, with their children. Today, they live with his 90-something mother Granny Rosie – also “Sussex to her bones” – who remembers watching cattle herded in fields where a supermarket now stands. In Granny Rosie’s youth, “the link between tradition and the natural world was present in every part of everyday life”, and that connection is the real focus of Mosse’s book. She has spent nearly all of her 65 years in Sussex. Her Languedoc trilogy was inspired by her time in the Aude city of Carcassonne, but it was Sussex that gave her a taste for the combination of landscape, history and storytelling that drives her books. The county’s folklore and countryside informed her gothic thriller The Taxidermist’s Daughter, and it was the backdrop for her memoir about family care-giving, An Extra Pair of Hands. Autumn gives us more of it. Walking under oak trees, Mosse pictures far off days when oaks were the only road signs. In her garden, she tells us that the Romans called wild cyclamen “earth truffle”, “believing that ill spells were ineffective where they were found”. If there is, at times, a touch of the guide-book in her telling, she wins your heart by the sheer joy she takes in the details. Mosse sets out what Sussex gave other writers, too. William Blake drafted Jerusalem in Felpham, then threw a drunk soldier out of his garden and was tried in Chichester for sedition (all because the soldier claimed he insulted the king). He was acquitted, but “never set foot in Sussex again”. cards.source_text: Actress’ music comes in fits and starts. That’s true of the songs themselves—which might be 20-minute slabs of ambient-leaning electronics or one-minute gasps of sharp, diffident funk—and for the way he releases them, with full LP campaigns punctuated by breadcrumb trails, short films, and download-only albums in between. His music follows its own strange, self-referential logic: Track titles are only vaguely comprehensible, and conceptual inspirations like chess and Milton’s Paradise Lost are flattened into his bit-crushed, hermetically-sealed sound world. The artist born Darren Cunningham is one of the most instantly recognizable electronic producers going, with a style—lo-fi, filtered, looping, limping—that has served him well for over 20 years. Enter Radical Frame, his 10th album. It’s brittle and uneven, beginning with two songs under 30 seconds long and ending with a 16-minute collaboration with Manchester rapper-poet Rainy Miller. Radical Frame is good, but it makes you work for it. The album is immediately disorienting. The first track is a manipulated voice saying “The Experiment,” stretching across the stereo spectrum as though it were being squeezed through a sieve. That’s followed by a five-second tune with a deep voice intoning,“Gimme the fuckin money, man.” From there it swings into one of the most brutal Actress tracks in recent memory: “Live By You” begins as a hard-edged yet melancholy UK rap track with CASISDEAD before Cunningham throws the whole thing down the garbage disposal, with rapidfire handclaps and harsh static swallowing up the MC’s voice. Then comes “Overchord,” with a nice piano intro and a soulful, vibrato-soaked vocal performance that feels dangerously close to veering off key before the track turns into one of those awkward house beats that Actress does so well, the voice resurfacing every once in a while like an especially persistent earworm. No score yet, be the first to add. Radical Frame is also difficult, which seems to be on purpose. cards.source_text: Beck rose to fame in the early 1990s as an absurdist poet who mashed together blues, folk, and hip-hop while getting crazy with the Cheez Whiz. For most of his career, that was the default Beck, the real Beck. But is that right? According to the forthcoming book The Last Temptation of Beck, he used to crash stages between sets, usually when one band was breaking down and the other was plugging in, and he’d play a few songs on acoustic guitar and harmonica for a captive audience. Some of those songs were straight-faced covers of blues standards and some were straight-faced originals, and they were generally received by a chattering crowd who were more confused than amused. It was only when Beck started rapping non sequiturs that the bystanders shut up and took notice. That was the first Beck we paid attention to, the one with the leafblower and Stormtrooper helmet, the one who announced himself on the Bong Load 7" of “Loser,” a surprise hit that caught even him off guard. The 1990s chose that Beck from several different mutations he was tinkering with at the time, and when he veered from that persona it came as a surprise. Mutations in 1998 and Sea Change in 2002 were both noteworthy for their attempts to express something personal in a more straightforward musical mode—the manchild growing up, abandoning irony and shenanigans—but those albums were just warm-ups for 2014’s Morning Phase, when Beck went full country-rock for a record that sounded like waking up after a dark night of the soul. Fans old and new embraced this new version of Beck, and none of his subsequent albums have landed with quite the same impact. Morning Phase reintroduced him as a commercially viable artist and even nabbed the Album of the Year Grammy. No score yet, be the first to add. Maybe a follow-up like Ride Lonesome was inevitable. After the more upbeat Colors in 2017 and Hyperspace in 2019, Beck once again picks up his acoustic guitar and dons his floppy folksinger hat. This version of Beck plies low-key musings about isolation and emotional alienation and arranges them in a way that balances loping country-folk with buoyant French pop (the bass is a lead instrument) and ’60s West Coast rock. With most of the musicians from Sea Change and Morning Phase returning, the songs settle comfortably into a familiar sound and a familiar version of Beck, right down to the relentless midtempo plod and the syrupy strings. cards.source_text: For music that is so unashamedly beautiful, there is something distinctly unnerving about The Meaning of Flowers, the fifth studio album from Danish singer-songwriter, instrumentalist, and producer Agnes Obel. The record, Obel’s first since 2020’s Myopia, reflects her experience of pregnancy and motherhood, with influences including Hannah Arendt, Danish pop music from the 1980s, and the soundtrack to Don’t Look Down. So far, so human. But The Meaning of Flowers wraps a deep humanity in feelings that are simultaneously otherworldly and profoundly earthy. Like the work of Enya, Clannad, or even Deep Forest, The Meaning of Flowers feels older than time, like music that has been excavated from a cave, or perhaps beamed from the stars. Central to this is Obel’s voice, which has a thick, almost smudged beauty that sits intriguingly between childlike innocence, aged wisdom, and the motherly hum of a warm synthesiser tone. Some of her vocals have been pitch-shifted, but it says a lot of their velvety, viscous quality that it is hard to distinguish between voice and effect. The massed backing vocals on “Laymelli” dissolve into the song’s synthesised string rush like a lazy river meeting the sea. No score yet, be the first to add. Similar to Cocteau Twins’ Elizabeth Fraser, the meaning of the words in Obel’s music is sacrificed to tone, creating a kind of primordial superfeeling that goes beyond language. Obel is singing in English—and the lyrics are poetic, when you decipher them—but most of the time you would struggle to recognize their origin, with only the rare phrase raising its head from the soup. Shorn of language, much of the music’s emotional impact relies on the vocal melodies. And they are frequently exquisite—see, for example, the casual turns and pointillist touches on “Laymelli,” the birdlike swoops and exhausted melancholy on the gorgeous “Gemini,” or the early morning film noir of the mysterious “Jenn’s on the Way,” a song whose faintly panicky air suggests, perhaps unintentionally, that Jenn may have nefarious intentions. Beneath this, the music lays the perfect bed. The Meaning of Flowers, which is notably more electronic than Myopia, was recorded in Obel’s home studio in Berlin, with the producer contributing voice, piano, synth, and samples and guest musicians chipping in. cards.source_text: Perhaps it’s just a strange coincidence that the leader of the Drin bears a name that reads like a stage-alias mash-up of two of the most iconic artists of the 1960s. But while Dylan McCartney’s band deploys a brand of sinister, post-industrial psych-rock that doesn’t feel reverentially retro, his artistic ethos could best be described as a case of Dylan vs. McCartney: He’s both the ragged raconteur gazing wearily out at our cruel world, and the ambitious, console-savvy alchemist seeking to transcend it. Since launching the Drin with a home-recorded cassette in the pandemic-clouded summer of 2020, McCartney has effectively built the project into a Buckeye State version of the Brian Jonestown Massacre. His prolific rate of output mirrors Anton Newcombe’s mid-’90s hot streak and occupies a similarly fluid position on the spectrum between jangle and drone, replacing BJM’s California-cult aura with a hardened Rust Belt resilience. McCartney has since surrounded himself with a proper six-piece band, simultaneously sustaining membership in fellow Cincinnati-scene pillars the Serfs and Crime of Passing. But all the while, the Drin have stayed true to his original mandate, tapping a deep well of record-collector touchstones (from classic and kosmiche rock to post-punk and dub to goth and neofolk) and reanimating them with a contemporary sense of unease—nostalgia as a gateway to dystopia. No score yet, be the first to add. For an industrious artist like McCartney, a double album is less a dramatic level-up than an inevitability. Clocking in at 23 songs and 75 minutes, I Lost My Way for Centuries is certainly the Drin’s most sprawling statement to date, but it’s also the most accessible on-ramp into McCartney’s psyche. And for such a wide-ranging record, there’s remarkably little fat. They don’t pad the tracklist with extended noise experiments or free-form jams; rather, each track functions as a challenge to work within compact pop-song parameters while still retaining the band’s improvisatory, wandering spirit. McCartney’s densely layered approach remains, but instead of plunging his melodies into a murky pool of doomy basslines, lo-tech electronics, and dubbed-out tape manipulations, he weaves thick tapestries from mostly organic instrumentation: guitars, drums, brass, shakers, and the occasional bouzouki. cards.source_text: Graham Epstein and Justine Dorsey are a match made in platonic-friendship heaven. The members of After—their anachronistic “trip-pop” band—were born on the same day in 1995; Epstein told The Cut that his pickup line after they matched on Hinge was “Do you like Creed?”; she listens to Addison Rae and he likes French Canadian black metal, but you know what, they both love Coldplay. They might’ve met in search of romance, but they were destined to be besties and creative collaborators: the musical equivalent of Delaney Rowe’s 2000s rom-com parody, which blew up on TikTok for its spot-on satire of its era. It’s cute, it’s endearing, it’s something. Like Rowe, After went viral last year for being scarily good at imitating ’00s media. The difference is that the L.A. duo admirably sees itself as above a gimmick; their mission, they told Rolling Stone, is to make you “miss a memory you never had.” Into this state-of-the-art cocktail of zillenial yesterday, they pour the pure ephemera of new-millennium breakbeat pop, the heartfelt edginess of Bush-era mall rock, and the fantastical normalcy of a Tucsan mom’s adult-contemporary CD collection. On their full-length debut, Fell Asleep in the Sun, After continue to survey these sounds and feelings—but beyond pretty, era-accurate production, they can’t muster the conviction or atmosphere to really take us there. This is a set of nebulous love songs whose melancholic narrative is spoiled by flat lyricism and unfulfilling pop arrangements. No score yet, be the first to add. As on their prior EPs, After’s ideas sound fascinating in theory but fail in execution. Epstein described the genesis of the duo’s songwriting process to The Cut: Dorsey would sing over drum loops from Akira Yamaoka’s macabre Silent Hill soundtracks, then he’d fit them with dramatic string arrangements. It’s exactly what we hear on opener “Take Me to Sunrise,” a song that could be about unrequited love or the album’s main theme of taking refuge in the past. Either way, the music offers little substance. Dorsey’s lyrics describe almost nothing about this “place [she’s] been before,” only that it’s “far away” and that we could totally “stay there if you want to.” Epstein and collaborator Jackson Shanks’ production should be there to fill in the blanks, but the stale acoustic shuffle doesn’t get the boost from those strings that it should—they’re hastily shoved into the hook and sour Dorsey’s gorgeous self-duet at the end. “Breathe Your Air” hits the Yamao

items.title: Doom Painting by AK Blakemore review – a dazzling epic of the Peasants’ Revolt
items.summary: This recklessly ambitious doorstopper follows the 16 days of England’s medieval uprising from a vast array of viewpoints, and in startlingly rich prose AK Blakemore’s third novel tells the story of the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, when commoners of all classes – not only peasants, but merchants, servants, smugglers, and some local lords and officials – rebelled at the imposition of a poll tax and rampaged through southern England, burning records of debts, killing their oppressors and laying waste to their homes. The book closely follows the events of the rebellion’s 16 days, employing a vast array of points of view, including the young king Richard II, several of his courtiers, dozens of elements of the rebellious Commons, a porpoise and a runaway horse. The title suggests the novel’s portrayal of these events as an inevitable reckoning; a “doom painting” was a picture of the Last Judgment on the wall of a medieval church. As a book of this scope must be, it’s a doorstopper. As any novel by Blakemore will be, it’s dazzlingly rich in lexical glamour, and this is likely to be any reader’s lasting impression of the book. Sometimes it feels as if the author is out to use every word in the English language in a startling, aestheticised, puckish way that expands both the word and the world. The result can be joyously silly. Who else would give us slugs that “blurb their elementary forms from out of the undergrowth to begin a dank and toothless festa ”, or “lunar-brilliantined mud”? But there is also gravity and passion here, especially when she intimately imagines the lives of the commoners: “they rise, to fry eggs in butter and pork fat; they rise, to whet knives on scarred stone; they rise, to braid the manes of their draught horses; they rise, to count arrows; they rise, setting aside their glitchy dreams of hairy stars and blue-skinned devils; they rise, fearful and powerful, into the bright day.” The cheekily anachronistic appearance of “glitchy” in this medieval scene
